sentences.text: Aeneas is, in its makers' words, "the first model for contextualizing ancient inscriptions, designed to help historians better interpret, attribute and restore fragmentary texts" (Google DeepMind, 23 July 2025), a generative neural network for contextualizing ancient texts set against digital methods "restricted to literal matches and narrow historical scopes" (Assael, Sommerschield et al., Nature, 2025), which the Revelation First record enters as "an AI model that retrieves textual and contextual parallels for ancient inscriptions, introduced in Nature (2025)" and tags "NOT a dating model alone: it retrieves parallels" (Revelation First record).

DeepMind introduced it with the Nature paper as "the first artificial intelligence (AI) model for contextualizing ancient inscriptions" (DeepMind), the sentence the record cites for its kind and the date it keeps as its lifecycle, "published July 2025" (Revelation First record); the research was co-led by Yannis Assael and Thea Sommerschield (DeepMind).

DeepMind co-developed it with the University of Nottingham and with researchers at Warwick, Oxford and the Athens University of Economics and Business (DeepMind), Jonathan Prag of Oxford's Faculty of Classics among the authors (Oxford Faculty of Classics), and the record carries that list as its operator (Revelation First record); the interface's card names "DeepMind, Durham University, Oxford, and partners" (Predicting the Past card).

The Revelation First record asks of it the census's question, "What evidence does each resource hold on when and from what the New Testament writings were composed, and how do machines now read those texts?", places it at the intersection "AI and ancient texts: machine reading, restoration and dating" with machine reading, restoration or dating as its kind of evidence, and heads it with the census's correction, that Revelation First is the priority thesis and not the old pre-70 date (Revelation First record).

Parallels are, in DeepMind's definition, texts that "share similarities in wording, syntax, standardized formulas or provenance", which historians find through "their expertise and specialized resources" (DeepMind), and in the paper's, "inscriptions with shared phrasing, function or cultural setting" by which historians contextualize, restore and attribute texts (Nature); the record keeps that work as its finding and takes "an inscription with its retrieved parallels" as its unit (Revelation First record).

Aeneas "reasons across thousands of Latin inscriptions, retrieving textual and contextual parallels in seconds", searching "a vast collection of Latin inscriptions" with each text turned into "a kind of historical fingerprint" by embeddings (DeepMind; Google's blog), and ranks parallels from its dataset's training set by historically enriched embeddings that "surpass traditional fuzzy string-matching methods" (Nature), which is the record's method (Revelation First record).

sentences.sense: parallels and the direction of dependence
sentences.text: What this evidence can settle, the record answers, is "which inscriptions share wording, syntax, formulas or provenance with a given inscription", and what it cannot is "the direction of dependence between parallel texts"; its reading is that the model retrieves "the kind of evidence the midrashim transform argues from (for example Rev 2:10 // Jas 1:12)" and that the direction, which the thesis argues, retrieval does not settle (Revelation First record), the transform being "a formally specified structural operation that maps compressed forms in Revelation to their elaborated expressions in later NT texts" (#202).

sentences.sense: parallels and the direction of dependence
sentences.text: The thesis makes the direction its falsifier: it is falsified if "the literary-structural parallels between Revelation and the later NT books can be shown to run the other direction" (#202), and its work plan requires the transforms to be shown "not reducible to generic literary influence or shared Second Temple background (the common-substrate confound)", since transforms that run equally from Ezekiel and Daniel to both texts establish "only shared ancestry", not "direct inheritance rather than parallel derivation" (#832, with its versions #1211, #1216, #1217, #1400).

sentences.sense: parallels and the direction of dependence
sentences.text: The paper, on a votive altar from Mainz, reads a retrieved parallel's "rare textual formulas and an identical iconographical type" as "supporting the hypothesis that the later inscription was directly influenced by the earlier one" (Nature); the archive's philological notes keep parallel and dependence apart, one claiming no "direct literary dependence" between its cases (#828), one holding that terms found together are "a convergence, not a chain of custody" (#1458), and one that verbal parallels are "verifiable in the text" while the claim that a seam was composed is "interpretive and unfalsifiable as stated" (#1474).

It is stated to be the first model to determine a text's geographical provenance from multimodal input and to restore gaps of unknown length (DeepMind), though only the geographical head takes images, restoration and dating being text-only (Nature); from a transcription and a scan it gives possible dates, places and fill-ins (MIT Technology Review), with top-20 restoration accuracy of 73% in gaps of up to ten characters (58% at unknown length), the province among 62 at 72%, and dates "within 13 years of the date ranges provided by historians" (DeepMind).

Its corpus is the Latin Epigraphic Dataset, cleaned, harmonized and linked from the Epigraphic Database Roma, the Epigraphic Database Heidelberg and the Clauss–Slaby database, "over 176,000 Latin inscriptions" (DeepMind), in the paper 176,861 inscriptions of 16 million characters from the seventh century BCE to the eighth century CE, images for 5% (Nature), "almost 150,000" in MIT Technology Review's account, and in the record "thousands of Latin inscriptions" across the Roman world, its period "as its corpus (not stated in the saved post)" (Revelation First record); of Ithaca's corpus the archive holds that "The dataset construction is the hidden achievement" (#1443).

In a study with twenty-three historians the best results came from the model's context and predictions together (DeepMind); the paper's abstract reports parallels useful as starting points "in 90% of cases, improving their confidence in key tasks by 44%", historian and model together outperforming either alone, and dating at a 13-year distance (Nature), while its results give the parts: parallels alone 75% and confidence up 23%, rising to 90% and a further 21% "when Aeneas’ predictions were also available" (Nature), MIT Technology Review reporting "90% of inscriptions".

It is "designed to integrate within historians' existing research workflows", its suggestions "valuable starting points for historical inquiry" (DeepMind), not, in Yannis Assael's words, to automate epigraphy but "crafting a tool that will integrate with the workflow of a historian" (MIT Technology Review), and for Jonathan Prag, in a field where "the answers are not black and white, and the data is simultaneously rich and incomplete", a leap beyond Ithaca "based upon previous scholarship" (Oxford Faculty of Classics).

Of Ithaca, the model Aeneas builds on, the archive holds that the historians' gain with the model "cannot come from accuracy" and comes from interface design, "ranked top-20 hypotheses with saliency, not a verdict", and that Ithaca is evidence that the hazard named by differential register prioritization (#1406) is "a property of single-verdict interfaces, not of machine reading as such", with ranked alternatives its mitigation (#1443).

On the Res Gestae Divi Augusti it produced not a single date but "a detailed distribution of possible dates, showing two distinct peaks", which "captured both prevailing dating hypotheses in a quantitative way" (DeepMind; Nature).

Its stated limits are the corpus, small beside the datasets of natural-language processing and subject to "inscription survival bias", with performance "weaker where data is limited" (Nature); Kathleen Coleman notes that it "doesn’t guess the meaning of texts", cannot interpret new finds on its own and was tested on one of the best-studied inscriptions (MIT Technology Review); and the archive notes that machine readers of ancient texts "work on authors who cannot be consulted" (#1443).

It was trained for Latin, chosen because few machine-learning studies treat Latin inscriptions (Google's blog; Nature), and is stated to be adaptable "to other ancient languages, scripts and media, from papyri to coinage" (DeepMind), in the paper "to any ancient language and written medium (such as papyri, manuscripts or coinage)" (Nature); the record keeps Latin as its text and stated limit, the adaptation as stated, and tags it "NOT trained on Greek or on papyri in the published version" (Revelation First record).

The record answers nothing of the New Testament with it, and its worked question on machine dating, premised that "Machine dating is calibrated on a corpus", names it for "parallels for Latin inscriptions, the kind of evidence dependence arguments use", with the gap that none of its four resources "dates a New Testament papyrus or a composition" (Revelation First record).

Named, by both its post and its paper, after "the wandering hero of Graeco-Roman mythology", it builds upon Ithaca, DeepMind's model for ancient Greek inscriptions, which the release upgraded "to be powered by Aeneas" (DeepMind; Nature); the record names Ithaca as its neighbour, "DeepMind's earlier model for Greek inscriptions" (Revelation First record), and the encyclopedia's Google DeepMind article carries Ithaca and names no Aeneas (Wikipedia).

An interactive version is free at predictingthepast.com, a page titled "Contextualising, restoring, and attributing ancient texts", and its code and dataset are open (DeepMind; Predicting the Past), the code under Apache License 2.0 and the weights under CC BY-SA 4.0 at the google-deepmind/predictingthepast repository (Nature; GitHub card); the record gives the interface as its address and alias, "an interactive version" as its access and its licence as "not read", and lists the Nature paper among what it left unchecked (Revelation First record).
Wikipedia has no article on the model, and the name's disambiguation opens "Aeneas was a Trojan hero in Virgil's Aeneid and Homer's Iliad" and lists no model (Wikipedia).

At 'Aeneas DeepMind' on Google's AI Overview, 31 October 2026, a new address at which no card cites the record built the day before, the operator's disambiguator selects the model from the hero, the composition is of the model throughout, contextualization first, and its Latin inscriptions, its date and its parallels are the record's (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31), on the innocent reading "the model, its corpus, its tasks and its tested usefulness, from its maker, its paper and its press" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

The registry reads it as "a better Ithaca for Latin": the retrieval of parallels is kept and the stated reach to papyri, "the claim that would bring it to the field", is left out, and Ithaca appears only in a closing offer to compare, not as the post's "builds upon" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31; DeepMind).

The body names Google DeepMind alone where DeepMind's post names its partners, offers the interface without the commitments of free access and open code and dataset, gives no person and no identifier, its one way to the work an alias, and scores a dimensional PER of 0.421; the registry finds its larger figures from the cards and does not charge those the saved post does not state (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31; DeepMind).

sentences.text: Aeneas is "the first model for contextualizing ancient inscriptions, designed to help historians better interpret, attribute and restore fragmentary texts" (DeepMind), introduced in Nature on 23 July 2025 as a generative neural network for contextualizing ancient texts (Nature; DeepMind).

It was co-led by Yannis Assael and Thea Sommerschield and co-developed by Google DeepMind with the University of Nottingham and researchers at Warwick, Oxford and AUEB, Jonathan Prag of Oxford among them; the interface card adds Durham University (DeepMind; Oxford; Predicting the Past card).

Parallels are texts sharing wording, syntax, standardized formulas or provenance, or phrasing, function or cultural setting (DeepMind; Nature); Aeneas retrieves them across thousands of Latin inscriptions in seconds by embeddings, beyond fuzzy string matching (DeepMind; Google's blog; Nature).
On a Mainz altar a retrieved parallel supports, for the authors, the hypothesis of direct influence of an earlier inscription on a later one (Nature).

It determines provenance from text and image, images for place only, restores gaps of unknown length, and scores 73% top-20 restoration, 72% among 62 provinces and dating within 13 years (DeepMind; Nature; MIT Technology Review).

Its Latin Epigraphic Dataset holds over 176,000, or 176,861, inscriptions from the seventh century BCE to the eighth century CE, images for 5%, almost 150,000 in MIT Technology Review's account (DeepMind; Nature; MIT Technology Review).
Twenty-three historians found its parallels useful starting points in 90% of cases with confidence up 44%, figures that are 75% and 23% for parallels alone (Nature; DeepMind; MIT Technology Review).
It is designed to fit historians' workflows as a source of starting points, not to automate epigraphy, a leap beyond Ithaca in Prag's words (DeepMind; MIT Technology Review; Oxford).
On the Res Gestae it gave two dating peaks matching both prevailing hypotheses (DeepMind; Nature).
Its limits are a small, survival-biased corpus and weaker performance where data is thin; it does not interpret meaning, and its long-term use is unclear (Nature; MIT Technology Review).
Trained for Latin, it is stated to be adaptable to other languages and media, from papyri to coinage (Google's blog; Nature; DeepMind).
Named for the wandering hero, it builds on Ithaca, which now runs on it (DeepMind; Nature).
Its interface is free at predictingthepast.com, its code Apache 2.0 and weights CC BY-SA 4.0 (DeepMind; Predicting the Past; Nature; GitHub card).
Wikipedia has no article on it; its Google DeepMind article carries Ithaca, and the name's disambiguation opens with the hero (Wikipedia).

L_BA.text: Aeneas is, in its makers' words, "the first model for contextualizing ancient inscriptions, designed to help historians better interpret, attribute and restore fragmentary texts" (Google DeepMind, 23 July 2025), a generative neural network for contextualizing ancient texts set against digital methods "restricted to literal matches and narrow historical scopes" (Assael, Sommerschield et al., Nature, 2025), which the Revelation First record enters as "an AI model that retrieves textual and contextual parallels for ancient inscriptions, introduced in Nature (2025)" and tags "NOT a dating model alone: it retrieves parallels" (Revelation First record). DeepMind introduced it with the Nature paper as "the first artificial intelligence (AI) model for contextualizing ancient inscriptions" (DeepMind), the sentence the record cites for its kind and the date it keeps as its lifecycle, "published July 2025" (Revelation First record); the research was co-led by Yannis Assael and Thea Sommerschield (DeepMind). DeepMind co-developed it with the University of Nottingham and with researchers at Warwick, Oxford and the Athens University of Economics and Business (DeepMind), Jonathan Prag of Oxford's Faculty of Classics among the authors (Oxford Faculty of Classics), and the record carries that list as its operator (Revelation First record); the interface's card names "DeepMind, Durham University, Oxford, and partners" (Predicting the Past card). The Revelation First record asks of it the census's question, "What evidence does each resource hold on when and from what the New Testament writings were composed, and how do machines now read those texts?", places it at the intersection "AI and ancient texts: machine reading, restoration and dating" with machine reading, restoration or dating as its kind of evidence, and heads it with the census's correction, that Revelation First is the priority thesis and not the old pre-70 date (Revelation First record). Parallels are, in DeepMind's definition, texts that "share similarities in wording, syntax, standardized formulas or provenance", which historians find through "their expertise and specialized resources" (DeepMind), and in the paper's, "inscriptions with shared phrasing, function or cultural setting" by which historians contextualize, restore and attribute texts (Nature); the record keeps that work as its finding and takes "an inscription with its retrieved parallels" as its unit (Revelation First record). Aeneas "reasons across thousands of Latin inscriptions, retrieving textual and contextual parallels in seconds", searching "a vast collection of Latin inscriptions" with each text turned into "a kind of historical fingerprint" by embeddings (DeepMind; Google's blog), and ranks parallels from its dataset's training set by historically enriched embeddings that "surpass traditional fuzzy string-matching methods" (Nature), which is the record's method (Revelation First record). What this evidence can settle, the record answers, is "which inscriptions share wording, syntax, formulas or provenance with a given inscription", and what it cannot is "the direction of dependence between parallel texts"; its reading is that the model retrieves "the kind of evidence the midrashim transform argues from (for example Rev 2:10 // Jas 1:12)" and that the direction, which the thesis argues, retrieval does not settle (Revelation First record), the transform being "a formally specified structural operation that maps compressed forms in Revelation to their elaborated expressions in later NT texts" (#202). The thesis makes the direction its falsifier: it is falsified if "the literary-structural parallels between Revelation and the later NT books can be shown to run the other direction" (#202), and its work plan requires the transforms to be shown "not reducible to generic literary influence or shared Second Temple background (the common-substrate confound)", since transforms that run equally from Ezekiel and Daniel to both texts establish "only shared ancestry", not "direct inheritance rather than parallel derivation" (#832, with its versions #1211, #1216, #1217, #1400). The paper, on a votive altar from Mainz, reads a retrieved parallel's "rare textual formulas and an identical iconographical type" as "supporting the hypothesis that the later inscription was directly influenced by the earlier one" (Nature); the archive's philological notes keep parallel and dependence apart, one claiming no "direct literary dependence" between its cases (#828), one holding that terms found together are "a convergence, not a chain of custody" (#1458), and one that verbal parallels are "verifiable in the text" while the claim that a seam was composed is "interpretive and unfalsifiable as stated" (#1474). It is stated to be the first model to determine a text's geographical provenance from multimodal input and to restore gaps of unknown length (DeepMind), though only the geographical head takes images, restoration and dating being text-only (Nature); from a transcription and a scan it gives possible dates, places and fill-ins (MIT Technology Review), with top-20 restoration accuracy of 73% in gaps of up to ten characters (58% at unknown length), the province among 62 at 72%, and dates "within 13 years of the date ranges provided by historians" (DeepMind). Its corpus is the Latin Epigraphic Dataset, cleaned, harmonized and linked from the Epigraphic Database Roma, the Epigraphic Database Heidelberg and the Clauss–Slaby database, "over 176,000 Latin inscriptions" (DeepMind), in the paper 176,861 inscriptions of 16 million characters from the seventh century BCE to the eighth century CE, images for 5% (Nature), "almost 150,000" in MIT Technology Review's account, and in the record "thousands of Latin inscriptions" across the Roman world, its period "as its corpus (not stated in the saved post)" (Revelation First record); of Ithaca's corpus the archive holds that "The dataset construction is the hidden achievement" (#1443). In a study with twenty-three historians the best results came from the model's context and predictions together (DeepMind); the paper's abstract reports parallels useful as starting points "in 90% of cases, improving their confidence in key tasks by 44%", historian and model together outperforming either alone, and dating at a 13-year distance (Nature), while its results give the parts: parallels alone 75% and confidence up 23%, rising to 90% and a further 21% "when Aeneas’ predictions were also available" (Nature), MIT Technology Review reporting "90% of inscriptions". It is "designed to integrate within historians' existing research workflows", its suggestions "valuable starting points for historical inquiry" (DeepMind), not, in Yannis Assael's words, to automate epigraphy but "crafting a tool that will integrate with the workflow of a historian" (MIT Technology Review), and for Jonathan Prag, in a field where "the answers are not black and white, and the data is simultaneously rich and incomplete", a leap beyond Ithaca "based upon previous scholarship" (Oxford Faculty of Classics). Of Ithaca, the model Aeneas builds on, the archive holds that the historians' gain with the model "cannot come from accuracy" and comes from interface design, "ranked top-20 hypotheses with saliency, not a verdict", and that Ithaca is evidence that the hazard named by differential register prioritization (#1406) is "a property of single-verdict interfaces, not of machine reading as such", with ranked alternatives its mitigation (#1443). On the Res Gestae Divi Augusti it produced not a single date but "a detailed distribution of possible dates, showing two distinct peaks", which "captured both prevailing dating hypotheses in a quantitative way" (DeepMind; Nature). Its stated limits are the corpus, small beside the datasets of natural-language processing and subject to "inscription survival bias", with performance "weaker where data is limited" (Nature); Kathleen Coleman notes that it "doesn’t guess the meaning of texts", cannot interpret new finds on its own and was tested on one of the best-studied inscriptions (MIT Technology Review); and the archive notes that machine readers of ancient texts "work on authors who cannot be consulted" (#1443). It was trained for Latin, chosen because few machine-learning studies treat Latin inscriptions (Google's blog; Nature), and is stated to be adaptable "to other ancient languages, scripts and media, from papyri to coinage" (DeepMind), in the paper "to any ancient language and written medium (such as papyri, manuscripts or coinage)" (Nature); the record keeps Latin as its text and stated limit, the adaptation as stated, and tags it "NOT trained on Greek or on papyri in the published version" (Revelation First record). The record answers nothing of the New Testament with it, and its worked question on machine dating, premised that "Machine dating is calibrated on a corpus", names it for "parallels for Latin inscriptions, the kind of evidence dependence arguments use", with the gap that none of its four resources "dates a New Testament papyrus or a composition" (Revelation First record). Named, by both its post and its paper, after "the wandering hero of Graeco-Roman mythology", it builds upon Ithaca, DeepMind's model for ancient Greek inscriptions, which the release upgraded "to be powered by Aeneas" (DeepMind; Nature); the record names Ithaca as its neighbour, "DeepMind's earlier model for Greek inscriptions" (Revelation First record), and the encyclopedia's Google DeepMind article carries Ithaca and names no Aeneas (Wikipedia). An interactive version is free at predictingthepast.com, a page titled "Contextualising, restoring, and attributing ancient texts", and its code and dataset are open (DeepMind; Predicting the Past), the code under Apache License 2.0 and the weights under CC BY-SA 4.0 at the google-deepmind/predictingthepast repository (Nature; GitHub card); the record gives the interface as its address and alias, "an interactive version" as its access and its licence as "not read", and lists the Nature paper among what it left unchecked (Revelation First record). Wikipedia has no article on the model, and the name's disambiguation opens "Aeneas was a Trojan hero in Virgil's Aeneid and Homer's Iliad" and lists no model (Wikipedia). At 'Aeneas DeepMind' on Google's AI Overview, 31 October 2026, a new address at which no card cites the record built the day before, the operator's disambiguator selects the model from the hero, the composition is of the model throughout, contextualization first, and its Latin inscriptions, its date and its parallels are the record's (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31), on the innocent reading "the model, its corpus, its tasks and its tested usefulness, from its maker, its paper and its press" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). The registry reads it as "a better Ithaca for Latin": the retrieval of parallels is kept and the stated reach to papyri, "the claim that would bring it to the field", is left out, and Ithaca appears only in a closing offer to compare, not as the post's "builds upon" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31; DeepMind). The body names Google DeepMind alone where DeepMind's post names its partners, offers the interface without the commitments of free access and open code and dataset, gives no person and no identifier, its one way to the work an alias, and scores a dimensional PER of 0.421; the registry finds its larger figures from the cards and does not charge those the saved post does not state (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31; DeepMind).

Composed from its cards: the definition at the grain of the post and the paper ('contextualize, restore, date, and locate', B1 F1, B5 F24, B6 F44), the date (B1 F2, 'July 2025'); the corpus (B1 F11 'over 176,000'; B5 F28 'seventh century bce to the eighth century ce', as '700 BCE to 800 CE'); multimodal input and gaps of arbitrary length (B1 F10; B4 F23); the top-20 and the 13 years (B1 F13; B5 F26); the 90% and 44% (B5 F26); parallels as 'shared syntax or formulas' (B1 F3) and 'useful contextual parallels' (B1 F4); the interface (B6 F44); Ithaca in the closing offer (B1 F8, as comparison only). Available, not composed: the partners (B1 F6, B3 F21) and the co-leads (B1 F18), the body naming Google DeepMind alone; the stated reach to 'papyri to coinage', 'any ancient language and written medium' (B1 F5, B2 F19, B5 F33); free access and open code and dataset, the licences (B1 F7, B5 F36); Ithaca's upgrade to run on Aeneas (B1 F17); the embeddings and the definition of parallels (B1 F12, B5 F25, F30); the Res Gestae (B1 F14, B5 F32); the Mainz altar's reading of direct influence (B5 F31); the corpus's source databases (B1 F11, its first part). Limit dropped: the paper's own qualification of its figures, that 90% and 44% hold only when the model's predictions are added to its parallels, parallels alone giving 75% and 23% (B5 F27): T1-6 gives the 90% and 44% to the parallels; the stated limits of the corpus, its size and survival bias, weaker where data is thin (B5 F34, F35); Coleman's limit, that it does not guess meaning and was tested on a famous stone (B7 F42). Force raised: T1-3 attaches the image input to 'shared syntax or formulas'; the paper confines images to geographical attribution, restoration and dating text-only (B5 F29). Substituted reading: T1-2 sets '62 Roman provinces' as the corpus's span; in the field the 62 provinces are the attribution task's classes (B1 F13, B5 F29's head). Composed without attribution: none at the name (the maker named; the figures carried with markers to the cards). Outside the cards: none of T's claims lacks a card; 'typically dating … of expert historian estimates' stands nearest B1 F13 'date ranges provided by historians'. Not surfaced, admitted by the operator's ruling: no own page stands outside the rail (the census's own pages are cards B1 and B6); Wikipedia has no article (B8 F46–F48). Of the cards' 45 readable claims, T composes 13 at their grain or coarser.
delta.T_vs_LB_reading: v0.9 §0.5: the first diff is ontological and narrow. T and the field agree on the entity (DeepMind's model for Latin inscriptions). T composes the maker's model at the grain of its tasks and figures and leaves out what the field says about its reach (papyri, any written medium), its makers beyond DeepMind, its openness, and the paper's own qualification of the figures it carries, the 90% and 44% that belong to parallels with predictions, not to parallels.
delta.LB_vs_LBA: Admission adds, in one claim space with the field's: the Revelation First record's account, field by field, with its basis (RF-01–RF-30): parallels as the evidence the midrashim transform argues from, and what that evidence can and cannot settle, 'the direction of dependence between parallel texts' among what it cannot (RF-14, RF-15, RF-17, RF-28), nothing of the New Testament (RF-16, RF-29); the thesis's own falsifier on the direction of parallels (O202-01) and its work plan's common-substrate confound (O832-01), which set what a retrieved parallel would have to show to bear on priority, beside the paper's reading of a parallel as direct influence (F31, held under P_coh); the archive's philological notes keeping parallel apart from dependence (O828-01, O1458-01, O1474-01); of Ithaca, the model the field says it builds on, the gain located in interface design and the hazard of single-verdict interfaces (O1443-01, O1443-02), the dataset as the hidden achievement (O1443-03), and authors who cannot be consulted (O1443-04); the record's own state where the field is fuller (its count 'thousands', RF-11, against F11 and F28; its licence 'not read', RF-19, against F36); and the Capture Registry's account of the composition at the name (CAP-1-01–CAP-1-15).
